title: Precious Pebbles in the Bag
statement:
Each pebble is labelled with one letter. The string precious lists the labels that are valuable; its letters are all different. The string bag lists the label of every pebble in your bag, one character per pebble.

Return how many pebbles in the bag are precious. Labels are case-sensitive: 'a' and 'A' are different kinds.

examples.why: Both x pebbles and the Y pebble count. The lowercase y is a different kind.
Every pebble counts on its own, not each kind once.

constraints: Both strings contain only English letters
hints: For each pebble you need to answer one question: is this label precious?
Scanning the precious string for every pebble works but repeats work. What answers membership in O(1)?
Put the precious letters in a set, then count the pebbles whose label is in the set.

explain.intuition:
This is the smallest useful example of trading memory for time. Without preparation, each pebble needs a scan of precious, which costs O(p) per pebble. Spend O(p) once to load the precious letters into a Set, and each check becomes O(1).

The same move shows up whenever you filter a long list against an allow-list, such as permitted tags or feature flags: build the set from the short list once, then stream through the long one.
steps: Walk through bag and count every character that is in set.
pitfalls: Lowercasing the strings. Case matters, so 'A' is not precious when only 'a' is.
Counting distinct precious kinds in the bag instead of pebbles. "nnnn" holds 4 precious pebbles, not 1.

solutions.title: Scan the precious list for each pebble
solutions.idea: For each pebble, check whether its label occurs in the precious string.

solutions.title: Set lookup
solutions.idea: Load the precious labels into a set once; each pebble is then an O(1) check.

followups: Labels are now any Unicode strings rather than single letters. What changes?
Labels are only English letters. Replace the set with a fixed-size boolean array. Is it faster in practice?
